World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Landmark WA triathlon hits 25-year milestone
World.content:
For a quarter of a century, thousands of athletes have flocked to Western Australia's South West coastline to compete in a weekend of endurance sports.

This year the Busselton Festival of Triathlon will record its largest field of participants in more than a decade.

Among them is 66-year-old Dennis Devereaux, who will race in a 2 kilometre swim, 80km cycle and an 18km run.

The festival has been held in the south west since 2002. (ABC News )

The Bunbury local entered his first triathlon in 1983 and helped to found one of the state's first triathlon clubs in Bunbury.

Starting with about 20 members, Devereaux said it was an early bid to bring triathletes outside of Perth together.

Today, the club has more than 300 members.

Dennis Devereaux says the nature of competition has changed and evolved over four decades. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

"There were three of us travelling around the state participating in triathlons," he said.

"No one was wearing helmets, no one was wearing wetsuits.

"We used to use whatever bike we had, they weren't always racing bikes in those days."

Overcoming injury

But a 2019 accident almost cut Devereaux's triathlon dreams short.

He fell 4 metres while repairing a yacht, shattering both his legs and requiring multiple surgeries.

In 2019, Devereaux suffered a severe fall that broke both his legs. (Supplied: Dennis Devereaux )

"I was laying in the hospital bed, not in a very good place," he said.

"I didn't think I'd be able to keep participating in sport."

Before the incident, Devereaux had signed up to the Sydney Marathon and was determined to not let the accident keep him from competitive sport.

Dennis Devereaux trains for an upcoming triathlon. (Supplied: Dennis Devereaux)

"I got a lot of advice from a lot of the Paralympic wheelchair racers," he said.

"I managed to borrow an old race chair. Once I finished I realised I could keep participating in endurance sports."

Despite 15 bolts, three plates in each leg and a fused ankle, he has continued to compete in marathons, triathlons and an ultraman event that involved a 10km ocean swim, 421km bike ride and an 84km run.

Growth of endurance sports

First held in 1983, WA's long course state championships were hosted at Rottnest Island, Collie and Margaret River, before finding a permanent home in Busselton in 2002.

Triathlon WA executive director Mel Farley said the number of competitors had grown steadily.

Mel Farley says the festival will see thousands of participants and spectators. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling )

This year nearly 3,000 participants will compete — more than 750 competing in their first ever triathlon.

"I think for a lot of people, the only activity they could continue to participate in through COVID was running," she said.

"There's been a massive increase in the number of people doing long distance running and I think that triathlon just tends to be the next obvious step for those people."

Swimmers take to the water during a previous Festival of Triathlon. (Supplied: Clip Media/Busselton Festival of Triathlon)

Ms Farley said the population of Busselton had grown significantly since the first festival there, and operating costs had risen sharply.

"Especially around traffic management, those costs have pretty much doubled in the last three years so that has had a huge impact," she said.

Devereaux will race in this year's festival as an ambassador, which he hopes will increase visibility for those racing in chairs.

"I see the joy that a lot of the junior wheelchair athletes get out of participating in races," he said.

"Hopefully it'll encourage a few people with challenging physical or mental conditions to know that they can still participate in sport."

World.title: Britney Spears to face court for drink and drug driving charge
World.content:
Britney Spears has been charged in California with driving under the influence of drugs and alcohol.

The 44-year-old pop star was charged with a single misdemeanour count of driving under the combined influence of alcohol and at least one drug, according to the Ventura County District Attorney's Office.

A representative for Ms Spears had no immediate comment.

Britney Spears rose to super stardom in the late 90s and early 2000s, but struggled with public scrutiny and mental illness. (Getty Images: KMazur)

The criminal complaint does not specify what kind of alcohol or drugs, or what amount, Ms Spears is accused of having used.

Ms Spears, who has since entered substance abuse treatment, was arrested on March 4 after she was pulled over.

The California Highway Patrol (CHP) said she was driving her black BMW fast and erratically on US Route 101 near her home.

Miranda Priestly makes a splashy return in The Devil Wears Prada 2 The Devil Wears Prada 2 drops the beloved (or loathed) characters from 20 years ago into a very different media environment.

According to officers with the CHP, she appeared to be impaired, took a series of field sobriety tests, was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence of a combination of alcohol and drugs, and was taken to a Ventura County jail.

She was released on bail the following day.

Police completed their investigation and presented it to prosecutors on March 23.

A representative at the time called Ms Spears' actions "completely inexcusable" and said it would ideally be "the first step in long overdue change that needs to occur in Britney's life."

In 2007, Spears was charged with one count of hit and run causing property damage and one count of driving without a valid California driver's licence, both of which were misdemeanours. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)

Ms Spears voluntarily checked into a substance abuse treatment facility just over a month after the arrest, her representative said.

Her arraignment is set for Monday local time.

Because it is a misdemeanour charge, she will not be required to appear in court, according to prosecutors.

Prosecutors said the case will be handled according to their standard protocol for defendants with no DUI history, no crash or injury on the road, and a low blood-alcohol level.

Britney Spears has been awarded a Grammy, six MTV Video Music Awards and a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. (Reuters: Lucas Jackson)

They said Ms Spears will be offered what is commonly known as a "wet reckless", which allows a defendant to plead guilty and get a year of probation, credit for any time served in jail, a required DUI class, and state-mandated fines and fee.

The offer is common, especially for defendants who have independently shown motivation to address their problems and seek treatment, according to the district attorney's office.

The singer has a home in Ventura County just outside the Los Angeles County line.

Her arraignment will be held in the city of Ventura, a seaside community of about 110,000 people, about 113 kilometres north-west of downtown LA.

Rebel Wilson says social posts true Rebel Wilson has told a court several social media posts targeting the lead actor on her film 'The Deb' are all true, on her final day of cross examination in a defamation trial.

The one-time teen pop phenomenon and "Mickey Mouse Club" alumna became a defining superstar of the 1990s and 2000s with hits like Toxic, Gimme More, and I'm a Slave 4 U.

Most of Ms Spears' albums have been certified platinum, according to the Recording Industry Association of America, with two diamond titles: 1999's Baby One More Time and 2000's Oops! … I Did It Again.

Ms Spears became a tabloid focus in the early 2000s, and a source of public scrutiny, as she battled mental illness and paparazzi documented the details of her private life.

Ms Spears was supported by fans who protested to end the control of her estate, career and personal life by her father and attorney. (Reuters: Mike Blake)

In 2008, she was placed under a court-ordered conservatorship, run primarily by her father and his lawyers, that would control her personal and financial decisions for well over a decade.

It was dissolved in 2021.

Since then, she has married and divorced, and released a bestselling, tell-all memoir, The Woman in Me.

Ms Spears has essentially retired as an artist in recent years, releasing only a few collaborative singles since her last full album in 2016.

AP

World.title: Remote health technology saving time and money for regional mums during pregnancy
World.content:
Stefania Panella is excited to welcome her first baby in just a few weeks after dealing with the worry and anxiety of being diagnosed with gestational diabetes earlier in her pregnancy.

Living in regional Victoria, the constant glucose level monitoring and care she required could have been challenging on a number of fronts.

But in her town, at Goulburn Valley Health, she was able to access remote patient monitoring technology, allowing her to enter her daily glucose levels into an app that is monitored live by clinicians.

Stefania Panella logs her blood glucose levels remotely. (ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf)

"Once I was connected to my care team, I felt so much more reassured that everything was going to be fine," she said.

The technology is saving many rural and regional women from travelling hours to regularly attend short appointments, often resulting in missed work, childcare issues, and travel costs.

"With the current situation in particular with fuel prices and the convenience of not having to travel for a pregnant woman, I think it's great," Ms Panella said.

Nurse Tara Jones monitors gestational diabetes patients remotely. (ABC News: Charmaine Manuel )

It has also made patient monitoring easier for health teams.

"The data we are seeing is current, whereas previously it may have been dated by the time we got to look at their emails," Goulburn Valley Health Diabetes Centre nurse practitioner Tara Jones said.

"It has actually reduced the number of programs we are using to manage these women, so it is starting to save us time in using it."

Turning a digital leaf

Hume Rural Health Alliance (HRHA) oversees the information systems for 16 health services in Victoria's north and north-east, and all of them are still operating without any form of electronic medical records.

But it has introduced a virtual patient monitoring system that allows each hospital to better "talk" to each other to easily find beds for patients closer to home.

Neelu Kaur is the chief information officer of the Hume Rural Health Alliance. (Supplied: Hume Rural Health Alliance)

Chief information officer Neelu Kaur said remote patient monitoring tools and live dashboards, similar to those used by the gestational diabetes team, free up hospital beds.

"We need to start expanding into this virtual, connected care," she said.

Australian health tech company Alcidion said the push for a digital shift is gaining momentum.

Kate Quirke says digital technology is helping improve patient flow. (Supplied: Alcidion )

"Laying the foundations for regional health care organisations to be able to take advantage of clinical efficiencies, and even in the future AI, is a proactive way to support patients," Alcidion's chief executive Kate Quirke said.

" You do not need to wait until you are fully off paper to start to get some of these exciting benefits around patient flow. "

She said the remote patient monitoring technology was also being used by health services in the United Kingdom and New Zealand, and was proving particularly efficient in regional areas.

Many regional Victorian hospitals still rely on paper records. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Electronic medical records

The Victorian government released a digital health strategy in 2021 to overhaul health technology in five years with a focus on reducing risks to patient safety associated with paper-based care, joining up healthcare records, and boosting virtual care.

Despite Hume's early success in virtual care, health services are still eagerly waiting to implement electronic medical records.

In 2024, the state budgeted $21.4 million to support the planning and rollout of electronic medical records across Victoria, including for the HRHA.

"We're supporting the Hume Rural Health Alliance to prepare for the implementation of electronic medical records, helping doctors and nurses provide more connected care for communities across the region," a Victorian government spokesperson said.

World.title: House vote ends record Homeland Security funding shutdown
World.content:
After weeks of delays, the US House of Representatives has voted to fund much of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), but not its immigration enforcement operations, ending the longest agency shutdown in history.

The vote followed a White House warning that temporary funding President Donald Trump tapped to pay Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and other agency personnel would "soon run out," leading to new threats of disruptions for travellers at airports.

DHS has been without routine funds since February 14, causing hardship for workers, though much of the Trump immigration agenda that is central to the dispute is funded separately.

"It is about damn time," said Democrat Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, who proposed the bill 76 days ago.

The House swiftly voted by voice, without a formal roll call, to pass the measure, bringing an abrupt end to the stand-off that began after Mr Trump's deadly immigration crackdown in Minneapolis launched a reckoning on Capitol Hill over money fuelling Mr Trump's agenda.

The vote comes with DHS under intense scrutiny and after Mr Trump ousted Kristi Noem as the department's leader, installing Oklahoma Senator Markwayne Mullin.

The agency has about 260,000 employees across TSA, the Coast Guard, FEMA and other operations.

End to impasse a relief for federal employees

Many workers were facing furloughs and missed pay cheques this month as the congressional stalemate dragged on. The shutdown came after last year's government-wide closure for a record 43 days. Countless employees have struggled with bills or simply quit their jobs.

Donald Trump sacked Kristi Noem as Homeland Security secretary as the political stand-off worsened. (AP: Alex Brandon)

In the aftermath of the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both US citizens, by federal agents during protests against the immigration actions in Minneapolis, Democrats refused to fund US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Border Patrol without changes to those operations.

At the same time, Republicans would not go along with a plan pushed by Democrats to fund TSA and the other parts of DHS without the money for ICE and Border Patrol. They insisted that immigration operations funding not be withheld.

After the shutdown intensified, with hours-long lines at airport security, the Senate unanimously approved the bipartisan package a month ago. Then the bill languished in the House.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, called the legislation a "joke".

The funding row led to long delays at US airport security checkpoints. (AP: David Zalubowski)

To break the impasse, Republican leaders in both the House and Senate decided to tackle the immigration enforcement funding on their own through budget reconciliation, a cumbersome, weeks-long process.

That meant Congressman Johnson was able to unlock the broader bipartisan bill for the rest of DHS.

House Republicans late Wednesday, local time, adopted a budget resolution, on a largely party-line vote, that focused on eventually providing $70 billion for immigration enforcement and deportations for the remainder of Trump's time in office. His term expires in January 2029.

Bill 'offensive' to ICE, Border Patrol

Congressman Johnson acknowledged on Thursday that, while he had trashed the bipartisan bill before, the new budget process ensured that the immigration money eventually would flow "with no crazy Democrat reforms".

"We threw a fit," he said. "We had to."

But not all Republicans were pleased. During the quick floor action today, Texan Chip Roy said isolating the immigration-related money on a separate track was "offensive to the men and women who serve in ICE and Border Patrol and are serving this country every single day".

The White House had urged Congress this week to act, warning that the money Mr Trump tapped to temporarily pay TSA and other workers through executive actions was drying up.

Markwayne Mullin had warned that Homeland Security funding was running dry. (AP Photo: Jacquelyn Martin)

Immigration enforcement workers have largely been paid through the flush of new cash — about $170 billion — that Congress approved as part of Mr Trump's tax cuts bill last year.

Others, including at the TSA, have had to rely on Mr Trump's intervention through executive action to guarantee their pay cheques. Most of its employees are considered essential and have remained on the job.

But with salaries topping a combined $1.6 billion every two weeks, Mr Mullin had warned the money was dwindling.

Today, in a social media post, he wrote that the shutdown, "NEVER should have happened."

Federal workers 'not political pawns'

More than 1,000 TSA officers have quit since the shutdown, according to Airlines for America, the US trade group.

Everett Kelley, national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, said that, while workers were "pleased that Congress finally stepped up to do their jobs and fund DHS, it is unacceptable that it took them this long to do so".

He said:

" Federal employees are not political pawns. They are not leverage. They are Americans and they deserve to be treated with dignity and respect. "

The go-it-alone strategy under the budget resolution process was the same used last year to approve Mr Trump's tax cuts bill, which all Democrats opposed.

With the budget resolution now adopted by the House and Senate, politicians will next draft the actual $70 billion ICE and Border Patrol funding bill, with voting expected this month.

Mr Trump has said he wants it on his desk by June 1.

AP

World.title: Police raid apartment owned by Annastacia Palaszczuk's partner
World.content:
Police have raided a luxury Gold Coast apartment owned by the partner of former Queensland premier Annastacia Palaszczuk.

Detectives and specialist officers searched Dr Vahid Reza Adib's unit on Goodwin Terrace at Burleigh Heads at about 11am on Thursday.

Police said in a statement a crime scene has been declared and investigations were ongoing. They would not confirm the nature of the investigation.

Dr Adib, a Brisbane-based bariatric surgeon, has been in a relationship with Ms Palaszczuk since 2021.

Vahid Reza Adib and Annastacia Palaszczuk pictured in 2023. (ABC News: Kenji Sato)

Ms Palaszczuk has this week been promoting her new memoir, The Politics of Being Me, including at an event at the Robina library on Thursday night where she took questions from the audience.

Ms Palaszczuk said she "was not aware" of any police investigation.

On Friday Ms Palaszczuk cancelled a scheduled radio interview with ABC Gold Coast.

There is no suggestion of any wrongdoing by Ms Palaszczuk or Dr Adib.

World.title: Sea creatures, strange finds and physical feats feature in WA photo wrap
World.content:
This April, we bring you pictures of an AFL great's hometown return, sea creatures in strange places and memorials of different kinds.

Here some of the best photos that illustrated our news coverage in Western Australia from across the month.

Crown whale

A grass-dwelling whale was a strange sight at Crown Perth. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

It is not every day you see a metres-long whale on land, but this inflatable cetacean was an unexpected guest outside the Woodside annual general meeting at Crown in Perth.

It was accompanied by several protesters who opposed the energy giant's gas operations off the northern WA coast.

Lab corals

Lab-grown corals being subjected to heat-stress tests. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

In WA's north, scientists from the Minderoo Foundation and Taronga Conservation Society are breeding more resilient corals to help restore the Ningaloo Reef, which has been slammed by record-breaking ocean temperatures and, more recently, Tropical Cyclone Narelle.

Reporter Alistair Bates visited their laboratory in Exmouth and snapped this photo of a coral in literal "hot water", with researchers turning up the heat to see just how much it could withstand before bleaching.

Fuel woes

Madison Young relies on her car to get to and from her job at odd hours. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

Like many across the country and the world, hospitality worker Madison Young has been feeling the bite at the bowser as fuel prices stayed high in early April.

Fortunately, prices have since started dipping back to levels closer to those seen before the Middle East conflict broke out, but cost-of-living pressures remain at the forefront for many.

Anzac Day

WA Governor Chris Dawson with Di Ryder after she delivered her Welcome to Country speech. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Perth's Anzac Day dawn service, like several others across the nation, was marred by booing during the Welcome to Country, delivered by veteran and Whadjuk Noongar Elder Di Ryder.

The heckling was condemned by many, including Premier Roger Cook, and key RSL figures including national president Peter Tinley, who slammed it as "disgusting" and showing "disrespect".

People came out in droves at one of the coldest Anzac Day ceremonies in WA. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Serving members of Australia's defence forces were honoured at the Kalgoorlie dawn service. (ABC News: Jarrod Lucas)

Elsewhere in the state, thousands braved the Albany cold to attend the coastal city's commemorations, while for those in Kalgoorlie, it was about remembering the fallen.

Death in custody memorial

Priscilla Kelly has been left devastated by the death of her daughter at Bandyup Women's Prison. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Perth mother Priscilla Kelly's face is illuminated by a candle she never hoped to light, at the memorial for her daughter who died in custody.

She was one of two inmates to die inside Bandyup Women's Prison in as many months, and the death has been called a "damning reflection on this country".

Police probe

The 13-year-old girl was left shaken by the incident on a Perth train. (ABC News: Keane Bourke )

In mid-April, video footage of an off-duty police officer restraining a 13-year-old girl on a Perth train was shared on social media and sparked outrage.

The girl, who can't be identified, sat down with the ABC to recount her ordeal, amid claims the officer used excessive force.

WA Police have launched an investigation into the officer's conduct.

AI fines

Some of Elli Figomnari's fines have been withdrawn, along with thousands of others. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Disability support worker Elli Figomnari has been facing the process of appealing fines issued by authorities using AI-assisted cameras on WA roads.

Four infringements she received related to a neurodivergent passenger, and while three of them have since been withdrawn, she is still dealing with the stress of the situation.

Those withdrawn fines are some of the more than $1 million worth of infringements withdrawn since the new cameras were rolled out six months ago

Cosmic debris

Dr Aaron Cavosie says australite finds are only reported once every year or two. (ABC Esperance: Andrew Williams)

Despite being as old as the geological equivalent of "last night" according to a planetary scientist, this 800,000 year-old cosmic debris known as an australite is a rare find.

Scientist Dr Aaron Cavosie inspects it closely, after Goldfields prospector Jim Miles brought him the object, which is made of re-solidified molten glass.

No-grounds evictions

Eleanor Kahlo left her rental home in April. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Renter Eleanor Kahlo left her home this month after a no-grounds eviction.

Her case was one of many complicated examples of no-grounds evictions, which are only allowed in Western Australia and the Northern Territory, and the details of her case were disputed on both sides.

April was also the same month that an Anglicare WA report revealed the state's rental vacancy rate was half the national figure.

Hometown footy

Lance 'Buddy' Franklin ran out for his first game for the Dowerin Tigers in more than two decades. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

To AFL fans, Lance "Buddy" Franklin is a household name, with more than 1,000 goals under his belt and two premierships in the can before he retired in 2023.

True to his roots, Franklin made a return to the Dowerin Tigers to play in the Wheatbelt town he grew up in, which was buzzing with excitement during the game.

Swimming world record

Andy Donaldson completed his record-breaking swim down the Ord River in just under 12 hours. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

History was made late in the month as ultra-swimmer Andy Donaldson swam 55 kilometres down the Upper Ord River in the state's north — setting a world record.

A feat completed in just under 12 hours, Donaldson described the final leg of the incredible journey as "really, really special".

World.title: Some say this saga of stockmen, spies and civil rights never ended
World.content:
Strelley Station is located about 40 kilometres inland from Port Hedland in WA. ( )

Two decades before Vincent Lingiari led the Wave Hill walk-offs, 800 Aboriginal workers embarked on a three-year rebellion that changed the Pilbara forever.

Now, on its 80th anniversary, descendants say the strike's legacy is in jeopardy.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article includes archival imagery of Indigenous people who have died.

It is 39 degrees Celsius on a bone-dry plain in remote Western Australia, but Bruce Thomas still sips from a steaming mug of tea.

"This is a memory from the past," he says.

The Mangala man is the eldest surviving son of Australia's longest industrial action.

And where he gestures lies its legacy.

Bruce Thomas is unfazed by the heat. ( )

Strelley Station is hidden in the desert like a secret.

To the west is one of the planet's largest bulk export ports.

Port Hedland's wharves heave with hundreds of millions of tonnes of iron ore, representing roughly 4 per cent of the national economy.

The sun-bleached town, 1,630 kilometres north of Perth, is last call for sailors bound for China, where the precious red earth in their holds will be refined into steel to build skyscrapers and car parts.

But only an hour's drive from the hum of global commerce, yellow-green spinifex and empty skies unfurl as far as the eye can see.

Follow an unmarked dirt path and you might stumble across Strelley.

Students are served breakfast before class. ( )

Lessons at the school are taught in English and Nyangumarta. ( )

Creativity flows at the school. ( )

Strelley is home to WA’s first independent Aboriginal school. ( )

There is a school made up of two light-filled classrooms plastered with children's drawings and Nyangumarta words.

Beyond that, an encampment sketched out among busted cars, bare mattresses and the ash of cooking fires.

"We all settled down here, big mob," Mr Thomas says.

" Government took everything away … they took the power and left us. "

Like many places in the Pilbara, Strelley Station is worth far more than first appears.

This is hallowed ground.

Bruce Thomas remembers the history of the strike. ( )

To understand what Mr Thomas sees through brown eyes ringed blue with age, you must go back 80 years.

To when the world was fresh from war, and the Pilbara's Aboriginal people were at breaking point.

The strike

Mustering sheep and cattle, taming horses and erecting miles of fence line in one of the hottest regions on Earth is brutal work.

From the 1860s until May 1, 1946, it was done almost entirely by Aboriginal stockmen, while women worked unremittingly in the homesteads as domestic servants.

They would come back to crowded quarters segregated from white people.

Few were paid. They were instead handed rations of flour, tea, sugar and tobacco.

The death toll on the Pilbara's pastoral stations was systemically under-reported, but first-hand accounts describe malnutrition, disease and harsh punishment.

The Strelley Station homestead, and Aboriginal stockmen circa 1940. ( )

A 1909 report by Marble Bar corporal CW Street recounts an influenza and measles outbreak that killed 18 Aboriginal station workers in a span of weeks.

"I am afraid it will carry off a large number of natives," he wrote.

"The station people all keep medicine chests and do all they possibly can for the sick natives.

" But they are most difficult creatures to deal with. "

Under Western Australia's Aborigines Act 1905, workers could not leave the property without the permission of the boss.

Defiance was met by the boot-heel of local police and "travelling inspectors", who marched dissidents through the stifling heat in chains.

Aboriginal prisoners chained by the neck for transport to the Roebourne Gaol in 1896. ( )

Then, on that first day of May, everything changed

Hundreds of workers walked off the job together.

The movement would swell to 800 at its height, and they would not return for three years. It remains the longest strike in Australian history.

Grinden Yougarla's father, Crow, joined them.

"He was one of the leaders," Grinden says.

" They're all my heroes for doing what they did. "

Pilbara strikers gather at camp. ( )

Staring through the iron bars of the Marble Bar police station, Grinden is struck by his late father's memory.

"I'm really proud," he says.

Known today as the location of Australia's lengthiest heatwave, the town of Marble Bar was at the centre of the Pilbara's gold rush in the late 19th century.

The stone cell Grinden surveys is small and dimly lit. It is being used to store police cruiser tyres.

Almost 80 years earlier, it imprisoned his father.

Grinden Yougarla visiting the cell that held his father. ( )

On April 14, 1949, Crow Yougarla was arrested at gunpoint alongside organisers Dooley Bin Bin, Clancy McKenna and 40 other strikers.

It was one of several mass arrests. The strike's leaders would spend months in and out of jail awaiting trial.

"They were brave and strong," Grinden says.

"If they didn't do that, I don't know where we'd be."

The Pilbara Aboriginal strike ended in November 1949 when Mount Edgar and Limestone stations were forced to break the deadlock, unable to endure another shearing season without Aboriginal labour.

It coincided with a ban on Pilbara wool shipments by the Fremantle branch of the Seamen's Union of Australia, turning the screw on property owners to make concessions.

The WA government welcomed mediation with promises of its own, however these would largely go unfulfilled.

The stockmen were left to negotiate their own pay until a full Aboriginal award rate was enforced by law in 1968.

Disillusioned, many of the strikers would never go back to their former lives.

It was into this new world that Bruce Thomas was born.

As an infant, he was carried from strike camp to strike camp, where his people set out to carve a fresh start from the Pilbara's rich mineral deposits.

Loading...

They formed small-scale mining cooperatives to eke out a living.

They used traditional methods to find their food.

As a young man, Bruce dug tin from the dirt.

"We got to make up the minerals, put them in a bag or a drum and send them back in a boat or a truck.

" Not enough tucker … we had to hunt. "

The ventures continued, attracting more and more people.

They came not only to work but to learn, believing the path to autonomy was through education.

For millennia, Aboriginal people had counted with the joints of their fingers and toes.

Now, they were learning the English words for these numbers.

Loading...

By the 1970s, the strikers searched for a more permanent place to settle.

In 1972, they bought Strelley Station with what they had earned from mining.

In four years, it would grow into a fully serviced community, home to about 800 people and WA's first independent Aboriginal school.

The strikers had wrested back some control, no longer made to feel like squatters on their own land.

The victory would not last.

The fall

One white man has an outsized presence in this story.

His fiery disposition both guided the strikers and drew the ire of a government in the throes of a post-war "red scare".

His name was Don McLeod.

The Meekatharra miner and communist emerged as an unlikely figurehead for civil rights. ( )

"My father, Ray Bulter, first met the activist Don McLeod in 1962," says Terry Butler-Blaxell, chairperson of the Nomads Charitable and Educational Foundation.

Ray Butler co-founded the foundation to support "the Strelley mob", as the strikers and their descendants began calling themselves.

"Don asked him for some advice on some mineral projects … setting up these mining camps to hack out a living," Terry says.

"Not much of a living, but better than living under slave-like conditions.

"They identified Strelley as a reasonable place to make camp."

Loading...

McLeod was a close confidante of senior Aboriginal lawmen Dooley Bin Bin and Clancy McKenna.

The flint-faced prospector from Meekatharra was also a unionist and member of the Australian Communist Party.

During the strike, he had met with the leaders in secret, out bush, because the Aborigines Act had banned Aboriginal people from gathering.

"There was always ASIO in tow," Terry laughs, referring to the Australian intelligence agency.

"There was always monitoring, always under surveillance. The state was very much paranoid about this man because, you know, he was leading a revolution.

" Are the Russians going to rock up here with a boatload of arms or something? "

Terry helps manage the Strelley mob's financial interests. ( )

The surveillance was so severe that a renovation years later would reveal microphones hidden in the ceiling of McLeod's office.

"It was real. They were watching," Terry says.

Alarmed by the strike's impact on the pastoral industry, state cabinet launched an investigation into McLeod's activities in 1952.

These interventions and repeated attempts to discredit McLeod only amplified his message, sparking a national conversation about civil rights in Australia.

Prominent social campaigners of the time voiced their support, including the country's leading feminist and only female ambassador at the founding of the United Nations, Jessie Street.

"Don't give up your struggle to help these people and don't be discouraged by personal criticism of yourself," Ms Street wrote to Don McLeod in 1957.

Despite the state's objections, the Strelley mob thrived.

Education was a priority for the community. ( )

They set up six more schools around the north-west. Streetlights were even installed at Strelley.

But the ripple effects of an economic boom would soon prove overwhelming.

Port Hedland ballooned by the thousands as it became a critical shipping terminal for recently discovered Pilbara iron ore.

Where there was once a tiny coastal community of 1,200 people in 1969, sprang an industrial thoroughfare of more than 8,000 by 1974.

To this day, Port Hedland is the Pilbara's second largest town and a focal point of its mineral wealth.

"Social externalities, that's an economic term associated with populations of miners, it brings all kinds of things that are not good for traditional owners, and those influences affected Strelley badly," Terry says.

Alcohol and violence began to break down the strikers, who for so long had stood united.

Terry is chairperson of the Nomads Charitable and Educational Foundation. ( )

By the time Terry took over the foundation from his father, the community was in tatters and its inhabitants scattered.

"Both state and federal governments determined that, well, Strelley was abandoned," he says.

"The state energy commission came in and ripped up the powerhouse, so there wasn't even any power."

It seemed long-standing animosities had come to roost.

Cars from the 1970s gather rust at the old Strelley homestead. ( )

The crumbling foundations of the old Strelley Station homestead. ( )

The cab of an old car. ( )

This is what remains of the Strelley homestead today. ( )

The fight

McLeod's combative and dogmatic approach had undoubtedly isolated the strikers from mainstream Australia.

Decades before his death, some within the Strelley mob grew tired of his repeated clashes with politicians and government departments, ousting his leadership of the Pindan mining enterprise he helped form.

McLeod died a pauper in 1999, one eye blinded by cancer. Hundreds of people from around the Pilbara attended his funeral.

He was buried at Strelley, a testament to his unwavering confidence in its self-governance.

"He was determined, absolutely bloody determined, and he wasn't worried about ruffling feathers," Terry says, shaking his head.

The true believers, who had followed McLeod to Strelley in the 1970s, shrunk in number.

Some succumbed to illness and old age, or relocated to better-resourced Indigenous communities in other parts of the Pilbara.

Some residents live in derelict caravans. ( )

Signs of play and decay make for a strange contrast. ( )

Many people have relocated over the years. ( )

One of Strelley's four-legged residents. ( )

Some sleep on bare mattresses in unfurnished rooms and sheds. ( )

With no housing but dozens of families, Strelley's grounds have become strewn with rubbish. ( )

For people like Grinden Yougarla, heading for greener pastures is not an option.

"All my family's here. That's why I can't leave Strelley."

He is one of dozens, Bruce Thomas among them, who still sleep rough at Strelley.

They are unable to give up on the country their ancestors fought so fiercely for.

There are no homes. Young families stay in broken caravans or out in the open air.

Their numbers climb during cultural events and funerals.

"We live in the shed … with all the mattresses and no house," Grinden says.

"Too many snakes, scorpions, centipedes."

Barbara Hale still shares stories of the strike with her students. ( )

Strelley woman Barbara Hale teaches at the school and helped design its bilingual curriculum. Lessons are taught in English and Nyangumarta.

Just two of the strikers' schools remain. There is one at Strelley and another in the nearby community of Warralong.

They are the oldest continuously independent Aboriginal schools in the nation, with a total enrolment of 70 students.

Barbara grew up on Strelley country. She feels like it has been forgotten.

"I still tell the kids, you know, tell them, show them where I've been," she says.

"It's really sad that a lot of people left, a lot of memories in this place.

"[I want] to bring my family back here. It's important for us to look after the community."

The hope

Countless Australians know of the Wave Hill Station walk-offs.

Gough Whitlam in 1975, grey suit pressed and white hair coiffed, trickles soil into the outstretched palm of Gurindji man Vincent Lingiari.

The iconic photograph of Vincent Lingiari and Gough Whitlam. ( )

It is taught around the country. The Pilbara Aboriginal strike, 29 years beforehand, is not.

A Fremantle-based not-for-profit aims to change that.

"We've done some lessons for year 6 and year 10 and we're hoping that teachers will pick it up," Remembering the 1946 Pilbara Strike chair Rose Murray says.

A Nyangumarta woman whose mother was forcibly removed from the Pilbara, Rose says stories of the strike connected her to her country despite growing up thousands of kilometres away.

She has been chosen to address a twilight 80th anniversary gala in Port Hedland to open an exhibition of sketchings and artworks by Strelley residents.

Rose says stories of the strike connect her to country. ( )

Learning modules about the strike have been created for years 6 and 10. ( )

As the scorching Pilbara sun heads towards the horizon, local politicians, mining industry heads and small business owners turn their attention to the stage.

"Strelley people … everyone who was on strike has always wanted that story to be told in the schools," Rose tells the crowd.

Her inclusion speaks to the present focus of the Strelley mob, rekindling the strike's story for a new generation.

The learning modules are available online for teachers covering First Nations history and civil rights.

"We hope eventually it might go into the Australian curriculum," Rose says.

"This [was] a really, really major event and people from the Northern Territory, not just in WA, learnt of this event and it did help create other movements and other actions."

It is a message she wants Aboriginal students in the Pilbara to hear the loudest.

Loading...

The scramble for natural resources has transformed the one-time sheep country into Australia's economic keystone and white pastoralists like Gina Rinehart and Andrew "Twiggy" Forrest into billionaires.

Yet as China's construction surge sent mining profits into the stratosphere, a 2018 analysis by the Australian National University found two-thirds of the Pilbara's Indigenous population had not materially benefited.

In 2025, the median age of death in the West Pilbara was 57.

It was the youngest in WA, followed closely by the East Pilbara at 58, and well below the state's median of 81 years.

"Our families now are struggling in different ways [to the strikers]," Rose says.

"We want our young people to know, look at the strength of your grandparents and your great-grandparents.

"You can use that ability to work, come together, talk, share our problems and find solutions ourselves."

Rose hopes lessons about the strike become part of the national curriculum. ( )

Terry Butler-Blaxell says he hopes reintroducing the strike's history to the Australian public will invigorate modern-day Strelley.

He has launched a petition to the state government urging Strelley's recognition as a gazetted Aboriginal community and calling for investment in social housing.

"[Strelley] is the first real Aboriginal self-determination movement," he says.

" How's closing the gap going? Not working, is it? I think you need to try something different. "

Bruce Thomas is next to step into the spotlight at the gala.

He may have been taught English by Don McLeod, but tonight he performs a song in his native Nyangumarta language.

He sings of his country's sharp jagged edges and its ferocious seasonal storms.

Loading...

"I was upset and dreamed I was really upset and went to pick up the rain, the clouds came, the lightning struck all over, the clouds travelled north…"

The displays around him describe the strike in the past tense, something that ended almost a century ago.

Mr Thomas does not see it that way.

To him, the strike, the people who were part of it, and the ideas that created it are very much alive.

In the faces of the children who continue to learn at Strelley, he sees the seeds of a thriving community.

"It's still going," he said.

" You can't live in the past … you gotta move along. "

Strelley kids enjoy a day at the pool in town. ( )

Joshua Crow, is Grinden's son and a strike descendant. ( )

Children continue to learn at Strelley. ( )

It's washing-up time at the school. ( )

Credits

World.title: Emma Thompson to star in a new film accompanying a live Australian orchestra
World.content:
It's not every day you bring together Hollywood royalty like Emma Thompson, a live Australian orchestra, and music inspired by astrology.

But a new orchestral experience in Sydney, centred around Gustav Holst's The Planets is about to do just that.

Holst composed The Planets between 1914 and 1917, decades before humans cracked the Earth's atmosphere. His music influences our understanding of the sky, especially on screen.

"The Planets sits at the intersection of myth, psychology and orchestral innovation," says conductor Benjamin Northey, who will lead the Sydney Symphony Orchestra's performances on May 1-3.

The suite has long influenced screen composers, from John Williams's Star Wars to Joff Bush's Bluey.

But in a world premiere for the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, Northey will conduct a silent film starring real-life celebrity couple Emma Thompson and Greg Wise, created by Dutch director Lucas van Woerkum.

Creating a film for a live orchestra

Traditionally, The Planets is used as a soundtrack in numerous films and TV shows.

Van Woerkum flips that tradition by creating a film to accompany the existing music.

LOSS explores the process of dying.

Greg Wise and Emma Thompson play the roles of married artists in LOSS. (Supplied: Sydney Symphony Orchestra)

"You'll see the person who's left behind and the one who's making the journey to the afterlife," van Woerkum says.

Thompson begged van Woerkum to join the Symphonic Cinema project after seeing the premiere of his earlier film featuring Wise.

"I was absolutely blown away by this synthesis of a live orchestra and film, [which] means the music enters my body in an incredibly profound way," Thompson says.

" I went to Lucas and said: 'Please, can I be in one?' "

Van Woerkum was so surprised, he had to double check that "the champagne didn't go to my head."

Films with a live orchestra are a regular concert feature, but Northey explains how Symphonic Cinema is different: "I don't have to adjust the music to the visuals."

Instead, van Woerkum will be sitting with the orchestra and control what appears on screen.

"Every shot of the film is triggered by me; I can speed it up or slow it down to bring it directly in sync with the music," Van Woerkum says.

Processing loss

Thompson says the on-screen couple in LOSS isn't based on her real-life marriage with Wise.

Emma Thompson in the silent film LOSS, premiered by the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, May 2026. (Supplied: Sydney Symphony Orchestra)

"[On screen], we were married and we were both artists. Greg was a photographer and I was a painter. You get the sense this couple is used to being in peaceable and creative silence."

Thompson adds: "They're not people of the word in the way we are. We never stop banging on and laughing a lot."

Thompson and Wise's experiences with grief early in life inform how they approached their characters.

Thompson's father died when she was 23, while Wise lost his best friend when he was young.

"No one really talks about grief, no one really talks about death," she says.

"We have a very uneasy relationship with death."

While Thompson wouldn't reveal which of the main characters dies during the film, she says that the couple decided to stop listening to Holst's music during filming.

" Music is so powerful that it would have affected how we played the characters. "

Planets with personalities

Holst based his seven-movement orchestral suite on astrology rather than astronomy, giving Each planet a distinct personality.

Loading Instagram content

Mars is the bringer of war, and Venus is the bringer of peace. Jupiter evokes joy and expansiveness, while Saturn brings old age.

"It's not just about the planets of the solar system, but human psychology filtered through astrology," Northey says.

If the music sounds familiar to you, that's because "so many screen composers have referenced it," Northey explains.

John Williams turned to Mars, the Bringer of War for inspiration when he wrote the music for George Lucas's first space opera Star Wars.

"Williams directly copied the big, full-orchestra chords at the end of Mars for the Star Wars Main Title," Northey says.

"You've got this relentless drumbeat ostinato, and a brass-led, militaristic colour that evokes war," Northey says.

Williams isn't the only composer who has turned to The Planets for inspiration.

Bluey's lead composer, Joff Bush, extensively quotes Jupiter in the episode Sleepy Time, during a dream sequence set among the planets.

Others have borrowed from The Planets too, including in Gladiator, The Right Stuff, Conan the Barbarian and The Man Who Fell to Earth.

Music that keeps expanding

Since Holst wrote The Planets, our knowledge of the universe has expanded dramatically.

Benjamin Northey has overseen many live‑to‑film orchestral productions. (Sydney Symphony Orchestra)

Pluto was discovered in 1930 and later reclassified as a dwarf planet. Space exploration followed in the 1950s.

Holst didn't revisit The Planets to add a movement for Pluto before he died in 1934, but others have taken up the challenge, including Leonard Bernstein and Colin Matthews.

In 2024, Australian composer Deborah Cheetham Fraillon added the most important planet of all: Earth.

Asked why The Planets still feels alive, Northey says: "This piece works on every single level. It's visceral, intellectual, cultural, and it has had a profound impact on how we hear the orchestra today; even just how we hear stories in music."

Even with a silent film featuring screen royalty like Thompson, "the music remains the most important thing, but the visuals are there to deepen the emotional trajectory," Northey says.

Thompson highlights the "double-helix" relationship between the music and the film:

" The music spoke to the moving image, and the moving image informed the music. "

Interview with Emma Thompson and Lucas van Woerkum by ABC Classic Breakfast presenter Megan Burslem.

Symphonic Cinema: The Planets will be performed by The Sydney Symphony Orchestra at the Sydney Opera House from May 1-3.

World.title: Rubber bullets flew and a police van burned, then a furious man pounded on my car
World.content:
NationalCrime Rubber bullets flew and a police van burned, then a furious man pounded on my car Hannah Murphy Updated May 1, 2026 — 8:58am ,first published 8:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains the name and images of a deceased Indigenous person. Alice Springs: We got the word Jefferson Lewis had been arrested just as I’d finally put my head down to sleep. It had been a huge day. We started it with Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family, sitting with them in their home in Old Timers Camp. They were still immensely sad, but were hopeful on what would have been the fifth day of the Northern Territory police and state emergency services search for the missing five-year-old. Community members protest outside the Alice Springs Hospital. Sam Mooy The young girl had disappeared on Anzac Day, and was last seen in the company of Jefferson Lewis- a 47-year-old man who had recently got out of prison.



Police immediately zeroed in on Lewis as a potential kidnapper, but it was only on Thursday afternoon that we got the news everyone had dreaded: her body had been found. We went to the crime scene, and among the buffalo grass contemplated how a tiny girl would have felt out here in the company of a near stranger. When we got back to our hotel, ready to finally turn in for the evening, shouts started up on the Alice Springs streets below. “They got him! He’s at the hospital!” A police van is set on fire. Sam Mooy



A woman ran over from another balcony to show me a livestream of people gathering outside the Alice Springs Hospital, surrounding the front car park of the building. Photographer Sam Mooy and I ran to our car and headed down there ourselves – and what we saw was described by one bystander as the “biggest thing” they’d ever seen in Alice Springs. Hundreds of people crowded the street, throwing things at police, screaming hatred for the man who had been locked away inside. Lewis had been taken straight to the hospital because he had been found by police beaten at a nearby Charles Creek residence.



Some in the crowd wanted blood, and demanded it. Photo: Sam Mooy Tear gas was fired into the angry crowd of protesters. Sam Mooy Photo: Sam Mooy Police responded by first holding the line and blocking all access to the hospital, but the shouts got louder, and bricks began to be hurled.



Officers ducked behind their cars, which had their window shields smashed and repeatedly kicked by what looked like young children. Men screamed for Lewis to be brought out – “so we can all go home”. Those in the crowd said they wanted to deal with him their way. They were furious with police for “protecting him”, and a kind Aboriginal liaison officer in his 70s who had been looking after the family and had consoled me earlier outside their residence took the brunt of their anger. Kumanjayi Little Baby. Soon, police began to respond. A woman used me as a human shield to avoid a rubber bullet being shot at us, and bodies collapsed around us as tear gas spread. I piggybacked a seven-year-old boy across the road and back to his mother as tears streamed down his face, crying out the pepper spray. I was soon to follow, coughing and spluttering with my hands on my knees as a kind man offered me some water in his car.



About midnight and after two hours of rioting, we called it and jumped into the car for safety, but then an irate man pounded on our hood and told us to leave. We didn’t understand his urgency until we saw a police car behind us go up in flames. It was hard to tell if the series of booms that followed was from the rubber bullets being fired, glass shattering or the interior of the police car burning. I could only watch on as another cameraman took a face full of spray, and had his eyes washed out by a journalist from another outlet. A bin was set on fire. Rocks were thrown at police. Men pulled shirts over their faces and children had water poured over their eyes. But still, Lewis remained inside. For all the screaming, throwing, crying – police have every intention of bringing the man they say murdered Kumanjayi Little Baby to justice. World.title: Epstein’s possible suicide note hidden from public view
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaEpstein fallout Epstein’s possible suicide note hidden from public view Benjamin Weiser , Steve Eder and Jan Ransom May 1, 2026 — 8:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: A suicide note purportedly written by Jeffrey Epstein in a Manhattan jail has been kept secret for nearly seven years, locked up in a New York courthouse. A cellmate said he discovered the note in July 2019, after Epstein was found unresponsive with a strip of cloth around his neck. Epstein survived that incident, but weeks later was found dead in jail. A Department of Justice image of Epstein in prison dated July 23, 2019, just over two weeks before he was found dead in his cell. NYT/US Department of Justice The note was eventually sealed by a federal judge as part of the cellmate’s own criminal case, according to documents and interviews. That means investigators scrutinising Epstein’s high-profile death lacked what could have been a key piece of evidence. On Thursday, The New York Times petitioned the judge to unseal the note, which, the cellmate, Nicholas Tartaglione, recalled, said it was “time to say goodbye”.



While Tartaglione mentioned the note on a podcast last year, the scrawled message has remained hidden from public view, even amid unprecedented transparency in the government’s investigations into Epstein. Since December, the Justice Department has released millions of pages of documents related to the sexual predator. Related Article Jeffrey Epstein Inside Jeffrey Epstein’s campaign to ‘disappear’ his criminal past online The Times has not seen the note and could not find it in the Epstein files. A Justice Department spokesperson said the agency had not seen it. But a cryptic two-page chronology in the records describes how the note became tangled up in Tartaglione’s messy legal case. The chronology says that Tartaglione’s lawyers authenticated the note, though it does not explain how. If it were written by Epstein, the message could provide insights into his state of mind in the weeks before he died hanging from a bunk bed. The Justice Department spokesperson said that in response to a federal law demanding the release of the government’s Epstein files, the agency “underwent an exhaustive effort to collect all records in its possession”, including those from the Bureau of Prisons and the Office of the Inspector General.



Epstein’s cell after he was found dead. US Department of Justice Countless theories Epstein’s death, at age 66, was ruled a suicide by the New York City medical examiner. But revelations of security lapses inside the now-shuttered Manhattan Correctional Centre have spawned countless theories about how he died and whether he was murdered. When jail officials asked Epstein about red marks on his neck after the July incident, he told them that Tartaglione had attacked him and that he was not suicidal. Tartaglione, a former police officer charged with a quadruple homicide, has long denied assaulting Epstein. Bureau of Prisons records show that a week after the initial accusation against his cellmate, Epstein told officials that he had “never had any issues” with Tartaglione and felt safe being housed with him.



Nicholas Tartaglione, Epstein’s former cellmate, show in a Department of Justice image. NYT Convicted in 2023, Tartaglione is now serving four life sentences. He is pursuing an appeal and maintains his innocence. In recent phone interviews from a federal prison in California, Tartaglione gave his account of how he came upon the note. After the July episode, Epstein was moved to a different part of the jail and briefly placed on suicide watch. Around then, Tartaglione said, he found the note in his cell, tucked into a graphic novel. “I opened the book to read, and there it was,” Tartaglione said: a piece of yellow paper ripped from a legal pad.



The note said that investigators had looked into Epstein for many months and “found nothing”, Tartaglione recalled. He said the message continued along the lines of: “What do you want me to do, bust out crying? Time to say goodbye.” The now-closed Metropolitan Correction Centre in New York where Epstein was found dead. NYT Tartaglione gave the note to his lawyers, he said, because it could have been helpful if Epstein continued to claim Tartaglione had tried to hurt him. The note was not mentioned in the official investigations into Epstein’s death, including a 2023 report by the Justice Department’s Office of the Inspector General. The OIG declined to comment. But the timeline document released as part of the Epstein files summarises the note’s journey through the justice system. It is unclear why the document, which is titled “Chronology” and refers to inmates and lawyers by their initials, was created or who wrote it.



Related Article Epstein fallout ‘Why couldn’t I see it?’ Painful and profound reality of the Epstein elites exposed The timeline says that on July 27, 2019, four days after Epstein’s apparent suicide attempt, Tartaglione met with “BB” – his lead lawyer, Bruce Barket – and told him about finding the note. When a guard said Tartaglione was not allowed to go to his cell to retrieve the note, Barket told his client to give it to the next lawyer who visited him, the document says. Barket then called “JW” – another lawyer, John Wieder – and asked him to pick up the note from their client. The timeline indicates that the lawyers tried twice in the next few days to have the note authenticated, without success. They did authenticate the note in late 2019 or early 2020, the chronology says. Barket declined to comment for this article. The Department of Justice released millions of Epstein files earlier this year, but the New York Times could not find the apparent suicide note among them. AP



“My lawyers at the time wanted to make sure, you know, I didn’t write it,” Tartaglione said in a July 2025 interview with podcast host Jessica Reed Kraus. He said they had “handwriting experts” examine the note. Related Article Epstein fallout Virginia Giuffre remembered as ‘hero to the ages’ on first anniversary of her death The judge overseeing Tartaglione’s case, Kenneth Karas, who sits in the US district courthouse in White Plains, eventually ordered the note to be turned over to the court, according to Tartaglione and Wieder. In an interview, Wieder told the Times that he drove the note to the courthouse and gave it to a clerk. He could not recall what it said. The note appears to have become enmeshed in a protracted dispute among Tartaglione’s lawyers, leading Karas to appoint an outside lawyer to look into the conflict, according to public filings. Documents related to the dispute were sealed in order to protect attorney-client privilege, the filings say. The judge eventually issued a brief order that disqualified Wieder from the case, citing a separate, sealed order that apparently explained why. Wieder declined to comment on the disqualification.



A court spokesperson declined to comment on the existence of any sealed document. Such records, he said, are placed in court vaults for safekeeping. Crisis support is available from Lifeline on 13 11 14. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. World.title: ‘Absolute anarchy’: Riot erupts at Alice Springs Hospital after accused child killer arrested
World.content:
Updated NationalCrime ‘Absolute anarchy’: Riot erupts at Alice Springs Hospital after accused child killer arrested Hannah Murphy and Heather McNeill Updated May 1, 2026 — 8:51am ,first published 10:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains the name and images of a deceased Indigenous person. Hundreds of people have rioted outside Alice Springs Hospital where a man accused of killing a five-year-old girl was being treated, in scenes the police commissioner described as “absolute anarchy” on Thursday night. Police fired rubber bullets and tear gas into an angry crowd of about 400 protesters who converged on the hospital shortly after Jefferson Lewis, 47, was arrested over the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby*. Officers received multiple calls about 9.30pm on Thursday that Lewis was at one of the town camps in Alice Springs and was being violently assaulted by a group of people, Northern Territory Police Commissioner Martin Dole said. Loading



Lewis had become the subject of one of the Northern Territory Police’s biggest manhunts after the body of Kumanjayi Little Baby* was found on Thursday by the Todd River. Dole said detectives who arrived at the town camp intervened and arrested Lewis, who had received “quite a severe beating” and suffered significant head injuries. The officers – who themselves were also attacked during the arrest – took Lewis to Alice Springs Hospital for treatment, and soon a crowd of hundreds had gathered outside. “Large crowds gathered at the hospital, up to about 400 people, and attempted to gain entry [to the hospital] to get to Mr Lewis,” Dole said. “It really descended into absolute anarchy.” The angry crowd could be heard shouting “they got him” and demanding police hand Lewis over to be dealt with by the community. Police were forced to take shelter and use tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse the crowd after protesters hurled abuse at them and smashed police car windows.



Police cars were set on fire and jumped on as the officers attempted to move the crowd along. The riot lasted about five hours, Dole said. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘I know you’re in heaven’: Mother mourns her Little Baby after tragic end to Alice Springs search “I understand there’s a lot of anger and there’s a lot of grief, but what we saw last night is just not acceptable,” Dole told Sky News on Friday morning. “The law must apply equally to everybody, and as Northern Territory police, we take an oath to serve and protect, and we don’t get to choose who we protect, and that’s what we were doing last night. To turn on emergency services, to turn upon the police, is totally unacceptable. “But it also doesn’t reflect what we’ve seen in the last week in Alice Springs – we’ve seen a community come together, stand shoulder to shoulder, do line searches, searching for Kumanjayi Little Baby ... to see what that descended into last night, and that violent disturbance is extremely disappointing.”



A police car was set on fire after a riot broke in Alice Springs following the arrest of a man over the death of a five-year-old girl. Sam Mooy Dole said Lewis was flown from Alice Springs to Darwin about 3.30am on Friday and remained in custody. “I think there’s a lot of grief and sorrow and tensions do remain high, but look, the violence from last night has been quelled,” Dole said. Kumanjayi Little Baby vanished from Old Timers Aboriginal Town Camp on Saturday night, with authorities alleging Lewis, who was also staying at the camp, had taken her from her family’s house as she slept. After five days of searching for the pair, the child’s body was found by police near Todd River, about five kilometres south of the camp. Her cause of death is yet to be determined.



Labor senator Malarndirri McCarthy, who represents the Northern Territory, called for community calm on Friday morning. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘I know you’re in heaven’: Mother mourns her Little Baby after tragic end to Alice Springs search “We need calm to come into this space and remember that there’s families who are grieving, and justice now needs to take its course,” she told Radio National. “There needs to be a proper process now in terms of this criminal investigation, and it must not be jeopardised by foolishness.”



She said the Albanese government stood ready to provide additional support if needed. Earlier on Thursday, NT Police assistant commissioner Peter Malley warned others about helping Lewis. “We say to the family of Jefferson Lewis that we believe he’s murdered this child. Do not assist him – get him to the police station, and we’ll look after him,” he said. “And I say to Jefferson Lewis: we’re coming for you.” The girl’s family released a statement on Thursday afternoon saying she was missed and loved, and that it was going to be hard to live without her.



“I know you are in heaven with the rest of the family with Jesus, and the Father, Son and Holy Spirit,” the statement read. “Me and your brother will meet you one day, we are giving our lives to Jesus. Kumanjayi Little Baby went missing from Old Timers camp on Saturday night. Rob Roy “It is going to be so hard to live the rest of our lives without [you]. “Ramsiah [the girl’s brother] wants to tell you that when he sees you in heaven, he is going to give you the biggest hug ever.”



Kumanjayi Little Baby’s great aunt, Rose Spencer, said she remembered when Lewis arrived at the community about a week ago after being told by members of another community, Yuendumu, that he was not welcome there. Jefferson Lewis. Police media “We trusted him as a family. He was in [our family], but not any more. We don’t trust people,” she said. Dole said police believed Lewis was helped to evade detection. The search for him was further hampered by the fact he had no mobile phone, bank account or vehicle, forcing police to resort to “1930s-style” shoe-leather policing.



NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said she had spoken to the little girl’s mother, who was incredibly distraught. Gallery Gallery icon 21 images Crime In pictures: Alice Springs riot “Around 200 people have worked tirelessly around the clock in searching for this beautiful little girl who went missing five days ago, five days every Territorian has had their heart in their throat, waiting for the moment that we got the announcement that she’d been found safe and well,” she said. “That news did not come, and it’s fair to say everyone is feeling this loss acutely.” *For cultural reasons, the name of the five-year-old victim will no longer be published, in accordance with the family’s wishes.

World.title: ‘Ahead of us’: ANZ boss warns of future impact of Iran war
World.content:
ANZ Bank chief executive Nuno Matos has sounded a warning over the economic risks that would arise from a prolonged conflict in the Middle East, as the bank delivered $3.8 billion in cash profits for its first half.

ANZ’s results on Friday said its March-half profits were 6 per cent higher than the same half last year. The banking giant, which is kicking off a round of profit results from Australian banks, said the war had not sparked an increase in financial distress among its business and household customers.

ANZ Bank chief executive Nuno Matos has sounded a warning over the economic risks that would arise from a prolonged conflict in the Middle East. Aaron Francis

Matos noted ANZ is the most international of Australia’s big four banks, giving it a “front-row seat to global developments,” and he said its customers were entering the energy crisis sparked by the Iran war in a strong position.

Households were starting to feel some impact from higher transport costs, Matos said, and some would therefore have less money for non-essential spending. He said hardship levels had not changed yet but it was also “too soon to say.”

World.title: While code wars rage in the east, Force and Bears are working together in the west
World.content:
SportRugby UnionForce While code wars rage in the east, Force and Bears are working together in the west Jonathan Drennan May 1, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ahead of their first season in the NRL next year, the Perth Bears have gained a couple of unlikely allies in the Western Force and Rugby WA. While the code wars rage on Australia’s east coast, there is a strong belief among the rugby union community in the west that not only can the 15-man game co-exist with the NRL, but also that they can help each other grow in a state dominated by Australian rules football. Former NRL Zac Lomax star has helped to drive crowds in Perth for the Force Getty Images Rugby WA chair John Welborn played in the Western Force’s first Super Rugby game 20 years ago, running out in front of over 37,000 fans at Subiaco Oval for the fixture against the Brumbies. The Force’s highest home attendance this season is just 6,659. Welborn strongly believes rugby cannot afford to be territorial in West Australia. “I think WA loves supporting a team against the rest,” Welborn said. “We’re an isolated town [in Perth]. I really hope that in rugby union, we can get behind that momentum of the Bears.



“I reckon most of the people who are rugby people, certainly in WA, who [will] go and watch the Perth Bears, it’s much, much more likely that their rugby participation is at a local rugby union club. “So we’re not trying to change a [Fremantle] Dockers supporter or an [West Coast] Eagles supporter to be a Bears supporter or a Western Force supporter. What we are going to be able to do is bring along the Irish, Scotsman, South African rugby union zealots, and get them to come and have a look at a rugby league game – and vice versa.” Chair of Rugby WA and former Wallaby John Welborn welcomes the Bears to Perth with open arms AFR Force chief executive Niamh O’Connor believes an alliance with the Bears can help both codes in working with the Western Australian government to build infrastructure in a state dominated by ovals, not rectangular football fields. Last year, the Andrew Forrest-owned Tattarang company, which owns the Western Force, said it was keen to embrace the new Perth Bears and look for ways to partner with the NRL side, potentially investing in shared facilities and a new ground. O’Connor confirmed the teams are already working closely together.



“We’ve been quite supportive of the Bears coming into market ... because it allows us to look at infrastructure in the west and advocate from state government for a lot more rectangular and community infrastructure,” she said. “We’re working with the state government on an infrastructure piece that supports both elite teams together and the community in the same way, with a lot more rectangular fields. That’s in its infancy at the moment, but the state government has been hugely supportive of it.” Andrew and Nicola Forrest have invested significantly in the Western Force since 2017 Andrew Meares In February, the Western Force announced it would move towards a not-for-profit structure, a transition expected in the second half of this year. Andrew and Nicola Forrest have invested more than $90 million in the club through Tattarang since 2017. O’Connor remains confident the Forrests are not walking away from the Force. “They will still remain very involved, and they absolutely adore Western Australia and the Western Force,” O’Connor said.



“This is about creating an ability to diversify some investment and allow state government to step in and help. So that’s been really powerful, and they’ve been very supportive of this process the whole way through.” Related Article Australian rugby Smiles and sledges as former NRL foes prepare for first rugby showdown The Force play the Waratahs in a Sydney blockbuster on Friday night which will showcase the battle between former NRL stars Zac Lomax and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii. O’Connor is open to discussing partnering with the Bears on fixturing next year to help maximise crowds for both teams. “At the moment, it’s sharing facilities because that’s probably the most pressing, but as we start looking at the fixturing for 2027, when [the Bears] come in, we’ll start looking at opportunities there,” O’Connor said.
